How these were simulated

The earlier studies (Simulation_Results.html) treated each wheel as an ideal speed tracker, which can't show a dead motor. These runs model the motor itself against a separate rigid-body truth model, and run Python copies of the firmware code at 100 Hz: speed filter, PI speed loop, current limit, duty cap and slew limit, wheel-command limits, allocation and null mode, the attitude controller, Owen's encoder-fault check, the new dead-motor detector, FAULT TEST, SLEW TEST and the DEMO LEVEL rest-tilt reference.

  • Motor: torque = stall torque × (duty − speed ÷ free speed). Friction 4 mN·m Coulomb (6 mN·m on the rubbing wheel A) plus viscous drag, i.e. a no-load current of ~0.2 A at 12 V. Packs differ: free speed 150 / 163 / 166 / 160 rad/s per unit duty for A–D (A's pack is ~1 V low), against the firmware's single 160.
  • Wheels: J 12% above the CAD value, for the motor rotor. Encoder quantised at 400 counts per wheel turn.
  • Table: "current table" = 0.08 kg·m², pendulum swing period 3.3 s (≈ 5 mN·m per degree), resting at roll −3.3°, pitch 0.3°, plus 0.12 mN·m of yaw drag (measured). "Balanced" = no gravity torque.
  • Failures: simulated = exactly what the firmware does, holding the motor at the zero-current (back-EMF) duty from the measured speed and the firmware's 160 rad/s, so a small residual torque remains. Unplugged = zero motor torque.
  • Attitude is fed from the truth plus gyro noise; the estimator was verified separately (≤ 0.06° roll/pitch).

SLEW TEST (stretch requirement)

SLEW TEST slews to four attitudes in turn. Roll and pitch are measured from level, yaw from the heading at the start. Each slew follows the shortest rotation (eigenaxis) on a smooth cosine profile, from wherever the table starts. The duration is the longest of 3 s, a 0.1 rad/s peak rate and a 0.02 rad/s² peak acceleration. Each target must hold roll, pitch and yaw within ±1° for 1 s, then for a graded 5 s hold. After target 4 the test keeps holding it until STOP, and the tilt safety limit is 25° while it runs.

What this means for the demo. On today's table, use yaw-only targets at the rest tilt that DEMO LEVEL reports (SLEW SET n <rest roll> <rest pitch> <yaw>). The ±10° default targets need the swing period raised from 3.3 s to roughly a minute (CG within ~0.02 mm of the bearing centre). Holding target 4 "until STOP" is limited by momentum: the 0.12 mN·m yaw drag keeps filling the wheels, so the fastest wheel reaches the 55 rad/s cut-off about 3 min after completion in the yaw-only case and about 2 min in the near-neutral case (extrapolated). The test then stops with SLEW_WHEEL_LIMIT.

FAULT TEST (requirement 3: detect and compensate a wheel failure)

What the firmware does

  1. Detect a dead motor (always on while Armed, wheel_fault.h). Drive effort e = duty − speed ÷ 160 is roughly motor current ÷ stall current. A working motor at effort e accelerates its wheel at about 800·e rad/s² (stall torque ÷ wheel J, less friction). Every 0.1 s the detector compares the speed gained with that prediction. A block with mean effort ≥ 0.2 that gained less than 25% of the prediction, in the effort direction, is "unresponsive". Two unresponsive blocks in a row (0.2 s) mean the motor is dead. A dead motor quickly earns large effort: its wheel coasts down on friction while the speed loop pushes the other way, and the loop's integrator winds up.
  2. Compensate. The wheel is taken out of service. The controller already allocates over any 3 wheels (minimum-norm), so the other three carry on with whatever is running: ARM hold, DEMO LEVEL, SLEW TEST or DEMO SPIN. Nothing else changes.
  3. Coast the dead wheel. EN and ENB are hard-wired, so "both PWM low" brakes the motor. Braking a wheel at 20 rad/s would dump its momentum into the table in ~0.2 s. The firmware holds it at the zero-current duty (speed ÷ free speed) instead, so it coasts down on friction over 1–2 s.
  4. Test it. FAULT TEST <A-D> [s] makes that wheel's motor dead after the delay (default 10 s of Armed time). Only the driver output changes: everything above it still sees the commanded duty, exactly like a real open lead. Grading: PASS = the right wheel detected within 1 s, attitude error (controller angle error, all three axes) back within ±1° for 1 s within 10 s of the failure, then within ±1° for a 30 s hold. While the test runs, the null mode idles the wheels at ±100 rpm (no net torque or momentum) so a dead motor shows up immediately. The failure waits until the target wheel turns at ≥ 3 rad/s.

Times are from the moment the motor died. "Peak error" is the largest of roll, pitch and yaw between the failure and recovery. "Back within 1°" can't be earlier than the detection: where the error never left ±1° it equals the detection time. The 30 s hold starts 1 s after that, so its worst value includes the tail of the transient. In the unplugged run the test does not know when the motor died, so the firmware grades recovery from the detection; the table shows it from the unplug.

The one case that can't be detected quickly

With the wheel bias, stored momentum can still leave one wheel parked near 0 rad/s (the bias sets only the sum of the four speeds). In the yaw-only slew on today's table, wheel A sat at 0 rad/s. Failed there, it was detected only when the controller next needed it, 2.1 s later (that run grades FAIL on detection time). Attitude was never affected: the peak error was 0.22°. A stopped motor that isn't asked for torque looks the same dead or alive, and it doesn't matter until it's needed. That's why FAULT TEST injects only into a turning wheel.

Running it on the table

  1. All four wheels in service: repair wheel D's encoder first. Losing one wheel of three leaves too few, and the firmware disarms.
  2. FAULT TEST A (or B, C, D; optional delay in s), then start the manoeuvre: DEMO LEVEL, SLEW TEST or ARM. You can also send it while already Armed.
  3. Messages: # FAULT TEST: wheel A motor now DEAD, # WHEEL FAULT A: dead motor ... coasting, # FAULT TEST: back within +/-1.0 deg ..., then # FAULT TEST PASS|FAIL ... about 30 s later. The manoeuvre continues.
  4. Real failure: FAULT TEST REAL, then pull one motor lead (or that wheel's pack connector) while Armed.
  5. STOP / DISARM end the manoeuvre; FAULT CLEAR (Idle) undoes the simulated failure and restores the wheel.
  6. Logs (SLEW_/DEMO_####.CSV) gain columns wheel_status (. in service, x failed but not yet detected, D dead and coasting, - off), err_roll/pitch/yaw_deg (controller error) and fault_phase. STATUS shows wst= and fault=.

Limitations and what to check on hardware

  • Motor constants are estimates. Stall torque (~0.24–0.29 N·m) and friction come from the Pololu datasheet class, not measurements. The detector tolerates ~2× error in either direction (healthy ratio ≥ 0.63 vs threshold 0.25), but a quick check is worth doing: TEST A 0.3 and look at the spin-up slope.
  • Stiction: a wheel that needs more than 0.2 effort to break away for 0.2 s is reported dead. In test 5, wheel C needed > 0.4 duty to start, so it may trip; it isn't producing torque at that moment either. Fix the cause (pack C, rubbing) rather than the threshold.
  • Coast is an approximation: with EN/ENB hard-wired, zero current depends on each pack's free speed (150–167 rad/s). A true coast needs one driver EN or ENB line on a spare Teensy pin.
  • Magnetometer aid: a dead wheel still turns and its encoder works, so it stays in the aid's wheel-state check. The aid gates (gyro-only yaw) instead of using a reference that assumed that wheel was elsewhere.
  • Not modelled: estimator errors in the loop, air drag on the table other than the measured yaw term, cable effects, and the motor rotor beyond a 12% inertia increase.
  • Hardware status: nothing here has run on the table. The Teensy power fault (TODO.md §0) blocks uploads.
